text: Cynthia Morris Sherman, born on January 19, 1954, in Glen Ridge, New Jersey, is an American artist known primarily for her photographic self-portraits, in which she portrays herself in diverse roles and imagined characters. She is the youngest of five children, born to Dorothy and Charles Sherman; her father worked as an engineer at Grumman Aircraft, and her mother taught reading to children with learning difficulties. Sherman has described her mother as good to a fault and her father as strict and cruel, and she was raised Episcopalian. In 1972, she enrolled at Buffalo State University, where she majored in painting but soon began exploring ideas that would define her work, dressing in various characters using thrift-store clothing. Frustrated by the limitations of painting, she switched to photography, recalling that "there was nothing more to say [through painting]" and that she could instead focus on an idea. She met Robert Longo at college, who encouraged her to document her "dolling up" process, which became the foundation of her Untitled Film Stills series. In 1974, she co-founded Hallwalls with Longo, Charles Clough, and Nancy Dwyer as an arts center for diverse artists. She was exposed to contemporary art at institutions such as the Albright-Knox Art Gallery, SUNY Buffalo campuses, Media Studies Buffalo, the Center for Exploratory and Perceptual Arts, and Artpark. Influenced by artists like Hannah Wilke, Eleanor Antin, and Adrian Piper, Sherman is considered part of the Pictures Generation. She graduated with a BA in 1976. Sherman works in series, photographing herself as a director, make-up artist, hairstylist, wardrobe mistress, and model, often in her studio. Her Bus Riders series (1976–2000) features meticulously observed characters, including the use of blackface, which some critics argue shows insensitivity to race, while others interpret it as exposing societal racism; American critic Margo Jefferson noted the work reflects a "stale visual myth." Other early works include cutout figures such as Murder Mystery and Play of Selves. Her landmark series, Untitled Film Stills (1977–1980), consists of 69 black-and-white photographs in which she portrays B-movie and film noir actresses in roles like librarians, hillbillies, and seductresses, set in streets, yards, pools, beaches, and interiors, evoking Italian neorealism or American film noir. The series avoids titles to preserve ambiguity, and her heroines are often alone, expressionless, and rebellious, challenging conventional ideas of marriage and family; the gaze in the images is typically from a male viewer, highlighting the male gaze. The photographs are 8 1/2 by 11 inches, displayed in identical black frames. Sherman used her own possessions or borrowed items as props, such as the doggy pillow in Untitled Film Still #11, and shot most in her apartment. The series is divided into distinct groups. In 1995, the Museum of Modern Art in Manhattan purchased the series for an estimated $1 million, and Untitled Film Still #21 was listed among TIME Magazine’s 100 most influential photographs. Sherman has appropriated various visual forms, including the centerfold, fashion photograph, historical portrait, and soft-core sex image, with early works like the 1980s Fairy Tales and Disasters series first shown at Metro Pictures Gallery. In 1980, she created Rear Screen Projections, a series in which she poses in front of rear-projected landscapes, often as "hitchhiker" or "runaway" types, emphasizing artifice and theatricality, continuing themes from Untitled Film Stills. In 1981, she produced Centerfolds/Horizontals, 12 large (24 by 48 inches) photographs inspired by fashion and pornographic magazine center spreads, initially commissioned but not used by Artforum’s Ingrid Sischy; she poses recumbent, often supine, and aims for psychological depth, sometimes feeling tormented by the characters. In 1982, she began the Pink Robes series, including Untitled #97, #98, #99, and #100. In 1985, she created Fairy Tales, using prosthetics and mannequins to depict grotesque, disturbing characters inspired by classic fairy tales, subverting idealized representations with vivid color, theatrical staging, and a focus on decay and psychological distress. In 1989, provoked by the NEA funding controversy involving Robert Mapplethorpe and Andres Serrano and Jeff Koons’ "Made in Heaven" series, Sherman produced the Sex series, in which she removed herself from the images, using pieced-together medical dummies in sexualized positions; Hal Foster described it as an effort to "erode the subject and tear at the screen," and Jerry Saltz called it "anti-porn porn," noting the use of pubic hair, tampons, and sausages in excretion. Between 1989 and 1990, she made 35 large color photographs restaging European portrait paintings from the 15th to early 19th centuries under the title History Portraits. In 2008, she created Society Portraits, featuring wealthy, older women in elaborate costumes, styled hair, and heavy makeup, posed in luxurious but sterile settings, with digital manipulation enhancing wrinkles and sagging skin to convey loneliness and anxiety. Sherman stated she is trying to erase herself rather than reveal herself, clarifying that people often misinterpret her work as revealing secret fantasies. Between 2003 and 2004, she produced the Clowns cycle, using digital photography to create chromatically garish backdrops and montages of characters. In 2010–11, her exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art included a photographic mural, where she photoshopped her face into decorative backdrops to explore reality and fantasy. Based on a 32-page insert for POP using vintage Chanel clothes, a 2012 series of large-scale images depicts outsized, enigmatic female figures standing alone before ominous painterly landscapes from Iceland during the 2010 Eyjafjallajökull eruptions and on Capri. In 2017, she collaborated with W Magazine on a "selfie" project based on the "plandid" concept, using photo-correction apps to create Instagram portraits. From 2019, she exhibited self-portraits executed as tapestries by a Belgian workshop. Sherman has also created fashion series for Prada, Dolce & Gabbana, and Marc Jacobs; in 1983, she made advertisements for Dianne B. for Interview magazine, with Untitled #122 being especially iconic for de-emphasizing clothing; she also created photographs for a Harper's Bazaar editorial in 1993 and the Post Card Series for Comme des Garçons in 1994 with Rei Kawakubo. In 2006, she created fashion ads for Marc Jacobs, photographed by Juergen Teller and released as a monograph by Rizzoli; in 2008, she produced the six-image series Cindy Sherman: Untitled (Balenciaga), first shown in 2010. In 2010, she collaborated with Anna Hu on a jewelry design. She returned to working with Teller on Marc Jacobs’ Spring/Summer 2024 campaign. In the early 1990s, she worked with Minneapolis band Babes in Toyland, providing album cover photography for Fontanelle and Painkillers, creating a stage backdrop, and acting in the promotional video for "Bruise Violet." She also worked as a film director, moving to film with her 1997 movie Office Killer, starring Jeanne Tripplehorn, Molly Ringwald, and Carol Kane, in which Dorine, played by Carol Kane, serves as a stand-in for Sherman, and both share an interest in arranging bodies in diorama-like scenes.

Cindy Sherman is a conceptual photographer whose work explores the construction of identity, gender, and social roles through self-portraiture. She often assumes multiple characters using costumes, makeup, and props to transform herself, challenging traditional representations of women in media and popular culture. Her early work, such as the Untitled Film Stills series, features cinematic references and portrays archetypal female figures, highlighting the influence of visual culture on individual identity. In later series, Sherman experimented with digital manipulation and grotesque imagery to question notions of beauty, fame, and social perception. Her artistic style is widely recognized for its critical approach to representation, blending realism with theatricality and making the viewer aware of the artificiality inherent in images. Sherman created the six-image series Cindy Sherman: Untitled (Balenciaga) in 2008, which were first shown publicly in 2010. In the same year, she collaborated with Anna Hu on a jewelry design. She returned to working with Teller on Marc Jacobs' Spring/Summer 2024 campaign. In the early 1990s, she worked with the Minneapolis band Babes in Toyland, providing photographs for the albums Fontanelle and Painkillers, creating a stage backdrop for live concerts, and acting in the promotional video for "Bruise Violet"; she also worked as a film director. Sherman moved from photography to film with her 1997 movie Office Killer, starring Jeanne Tripplehorn, Molly Ringwald, and Carol Kane, in which Dorine, played by Carol Kane, serves as a stand-in for Sherman, reflecting their shared interest in arranging bodies in diorama-like scenes. According to author Dahlia Schweitzer, Office Killer is a comedy, horror, melodrama, noir, feminist statement, and art piece, featuring artistically executed murder scenes reminiscent of her Untitled Horror series. The film grossed $37,446 and received poor reviews, described as "crude" and "laugh-free," with art critic Roberta Smith noting it lacks the artist's usual finesse and calling it a "fascinating if lumpish bit of Shermaniana," while Stephen Holden called it "sadly inept." Sherman had a cameo in John Waters' film Pecker and appeared in The Feature in 2008, starring her ex-husband Michel Auder, which won a New Vision Award. In 2009, Paul Hasegawa-Overacker and Tom Donahue completed a documentary, Guest of Cindy Sherman, about their relationship with Sherman, which she initially supported but later opposed. In the catalog essay by Philipp Kaiser for Sherman's 2016 exhibition at Metro Pictures Gallery, he noted six short films she made in college that preceded Office Killer, and included a conversation between Sherman and Sofia Coppola in which Sherman admitted she may star in an upcoming film project. Sherman's first solo show in New York was at The Kitchen in 1980, and her photographs were the first show at the newly opened Metro Pictures Gallery that year. "Untitled Film Stills" were first shown at Artists Space, where Sherman was a receptionist. Her first solo exhibitions in France were presented by Galerie Chantal Crousel in Paris. Sherman has participated in many international events, including SITE Santa Fe (2004), the Venice Biennale (1982, 1995), and five Whitney Biennials. Her work has been featured in solo exhibitions at the Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam (1982), Whitney Museum of American Art in New York (1987), Kunsthalle Basel (1991), Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden in Washington, D.C. (1995), San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (1998), Serpentine Gallery in London and the Scottish National Gallery of Modern Art (2003), and Martin-Gropius-Bau in Berlin (2007). Major retrospectives have been organized by the Museum Boymans-van Beuningen in Rotterdam (1996), the Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles and the Museum of Modern Art in New York (1997), sponsored by Madonna, and Kunsthaus Bregenz, Austria, Louisiana Museum for Moderne Kunst, Denmark, and Jeu de Paume in Paris (2006–2007). In 2009, she was included in "The Pictures Generation, 1974–1984" at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. In 2012, the Museum of Modern Art mounted a show chronicling her work from the mid-1970s, including over 170 photographs, which traveled to the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art and the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis. In 2013, she was invited to organize a show at the Venice Biennale. In 2016, after a sabbatical spent "coming to terms with health issues and getting older," Sherman produced and staged her first photo gallery in five years, the series "The Imitation of Life," named after a 1959 Douglas Sirk melodrama, which presents her in highly stylized glamour portraits inspired by old Hollywood divas such as Gloria Swanson, Mary Pickford, and Ruby Keeler. The series was exhibited at Metro Pictures Gallery in New York City and the Broad Museum in Los Angeles in 2016, and later at Spruth Magers in Berlin and the Wexner Center for the Arts in Columbus, Ohio in 2017. In 2019, the National Portrait Gallery in London organized a major retrospective of her work from the mid-1970s to the present. In 2024, at the Goulandris Museum of Cycladic Art in Athens, Sherman held her first exhibition in Greece, gathering over a hundred of her early works. In 2024, at Fotografiska Stockholm, she exhibited Tapestries, a series of tapestries based on her digitally altered Instagram selfies, marking her first major exploration of this medium. In her Imitation of Life series, Sherman poses in vintage costume and theatrical makeup as various ageing actress-like women. Scholar Douglas Crimp describes her work as a "hybrid of photography and performance art that reveals femininity to be an effect of representation." Sherman does not consider her work or herself to be feminist, stating "The work is what it is and hopefully it's seen as feminist work, or feminist-advised work, but I'm not going to go around espousing theoretical bullshit about feminist stuff." Many scholars emphasize the relationship between her work and the concept of the gaze, particularly Laura Mulvey's analysis of the male gaze in relation to her Untitled series, where she notes that "the accouterments of the feminine struggle to conform to a facade of desirability haunt Sherman's iconography," functioning as a parody of different voyeurisms. Others question whether this confrontation with the male gaze and the feminine struggle was intentional, and whether such intentionality is important in understanding the feminist standpoint of her photography. Sherman herself has expressed uncertainty about the Untitled series' relationship with the male gaze, stating in a 1991 interview with David Brittain that she did not analyze it at the time as a feminist issue, though now she has mixed feelings about the series being too reminiscent of original pin-up images. Her work is also analyzed through the lens of abjection, with scholars like Hal Foster and Laura Mulvey interpreting her use of the grotesque in projects like Vomit Pictures as de-fetishizing the female body. Scholar Michele Meager interprets Sherman as having been "crowned a resistant celebrity" to feminist theory. In 2010, Sherman's nearly six-foot-tall chromogenic color print Untitled#153 (1985), featuring her as a mud-caked corpse, was sold by Phillips de Pury & Company for $2.7 million, near the $3 million high estimate. In 2011, a print of Untitled#96 sold for $3.89 million at Christie's, making it the most expensive photograph at that time. Sherman was represented by Metro Pictures for 40 years and by Sprüth Magers before moving to Hauser & Wirth in 2021. In April 2023, Phillips NY auctioned Untitled #546 (2010), sized 159 cm x 359 cm, for $355,600, well above estimate. Sherman's work is credited as a major influence on contemporary portrait photographers, including Ryan Trecartin, and extends to artists in other mediums such as painter Lisa Yuskavage, visual artist Jillian Mayer, and performance artist Tracey Ullman. In April 2014, actor and artist James Franco exhibited a series of photographs at the Pace Gallery called New Film Stills, restaging twenty-nine images from Sherman's Untitled Film Stills, which received mainly negative reviews, calling the appropriations 'sophomoric,' 'sexist,' and 'embarrassingly clueless.' Sherman lived with artist Robert Longo from 1974 to 1980, who also included her in his 'Men in the Cities' series. She married director Michel Auder in 1984, making her stepmother to Auder's daughter Alexandra and her half-sister Gaby Hoffmann; they divorced in 1999. She was in a five-year relationship with Paul Hasegawa-Overacker, creator of the documentary Guest of Cindy Sherman, and from 2007 to 2011 had a relationship with artist David Byrne. Between 1991 and 2005, Sherman lived in a fifth-floor co-op loft at 84 Mercer Street in Manhattan's Soho neighborhood, which she later sold to actor Hank Azaria. She bought two floors in a 10-story condo building overlooking the Hudson River in West Soho and currently uses one as her apartment and the other as her studio and office. For many years, she spent her summers in the Catskill Mountains. In 2000, she purchased songwriter Marvin Hamlisch's 4,200-square-foot house on 0.4 acre in Sag Harbor for $1.5 million. She later acquired a 19th-century home on a ten-acre waterfront property on Accabonac Harbor in East Hampton, New York. Sherman has expressed contempt for social media platforms, calling them "so vulgar," yet maintains an active Instagram account featuring her selfies. She serves on the artistic advisory committee of the Stephen Petronio Company in New York City and on the Artists Committee of the Americans for the Arts. Along with David Byrne, she was a member of Portugal's Estoril Film Festival jury in 2009. In 2012, she joined Yoko Ono and nearly 150 other artists in founding Artists Against Fracking. In 2023, Sherman served on the jury that selected Sarah Lucas as the first winner of the New Museum's $400,000 Hostetler/Wrigley Sculpture Award. Ahead of the 2024 United States presidential election, she was one of 165 leading contemporary artists who contributed pieces to Artists for Kamala, an online sale with all proceeds going directly to Kamala Harris' campaign. Her works are held in various collections.
